justification: #1197 suffixes a repeated ref_number with ~2/~3 so neither provision is lost. Its PR body states that citation_proof.split_ref 'ignores the suffix'. It does not: it ignores it only in the shape #1197 tested, where an item marker separates the marker from the digits. Attached straight to a clause number the marker eats the last component, so a marked row's clause number is judged against its PARENT clause, never proves, and citation_status withholds a number the council did print. Measured, not reasoned: five rows in the 2026-10-02 City of Sydney re-read were held as 'citation not proven on its source page' while their own numbers are printed on their own pages. One line of regex in a pure string function, plus the regression test. TWO MORE CHANGES, both forced by the same City of Sydney re-read and both ruled on by the user. (a) ai_extractor.drop_figure_narrations refuses a provision whose body OPENS by reporting what a drawing shows: six Schedule 6 sections came back as the reader's own sentences with measurements read off artwork ("The drawing shows WP1 wall plaques on the front wall"), and nothing like it is live, so approving them would have put new sentences in the council's mouth. (b) page_coverage.skipped_pages now scores a page's RULE-BEARING lines instead of every sentence line. Page 65 of schedules prints clause 11.2(10)(a)-(d) and then 30 lines of commentary about AS 4282-1997: 47 sentence lines, 7 rule-bearing. A correct extraction matches all 7 and misses nothing, yet scored 14/47 = 0.2979 against PAGE_HIT 0.3 and was refused by ONE line, four times across two sessions, for returning exactly what it should.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: The marker strip is removed. Forced, not predicted: with code_groups restored to its pre-fix body, 3 of the test's 4 marked/unmarked pairs break - 3_15_5_2~2 reads ['3.15.5'] against its twin's ['3.15.5.2'], 3_1_1~4 reads ['3.1'] against ['3.1.1'], and 3_15~6 reads [] ('bare integer section, not discriminating') against ['3.15']. The fourth pair, 7_4 (a)~2, passes either way, which is exactly why #1197's reasoning looked sound: its own example is the one shape the bug does not touch. With the fix: 41 passed, 1 xfailed.
falsifiable_check.external_authority: The council's own PDF, not our own output. Sydney DCP 2012 section-3-general-provisions, R2 v1.2-2026-10-01, sha256 f225b89b0c82ca484119f0950f09e26c1aedcff07d927dc545046c72c363af2b, verified equal to dcp_chapter_registry.content_hash for that chapter. Page 106 prints '3.15.5.2 Monitoring and Review' verbatim, so row 3_15_5_2~2's clause number was correct and the verdict against it was not. On the live queue the fix moved exactly 5 rows from held to grounded and left the other 18 held, so it did not simply loosen the gate.
falsifiable_check.observed_red: Watched red before the fix, pasted as printed. With code_groups restored to its pre-fix body the pairing assertions print: "3_15_5_2~2 -> ['3.15.5'] vs twin 3_15_5_2 -> ['3.15.5.2']", "3_1_1~4 -> ['3.1'] vs twin 3_1_1 -> ['3.1.1']", "3_15~6 -> [] vs twin 3_15 -> ['3.15']", and "assertions broken: 3 of 4 pairs". The live gate printed it too, before anything was edited: dcp_approve_graded.py --council city_of_sydney reported "LEFT PENDING for a person : 23 / 23 clause number not proven on its source page", and after the fix and re-grade "pending rows in scope : 23 / to approve : 5 / 5 grounded / LEFT PENDING for a person : 18".

pre_impl.existing_data: frontend-nextjs/lib/citation-display.ts already strips this marker with /~\d+$/ before any label is shown (#1197). The Python side had no equivalent, which is the whole defect - the two sides read different clause numbers from the same ref. The marker is written in dcp_extract_changed.diff_provisions at line 4032 (ref = f'{ref}~{suffix}'). No new concept and no new constant: the strip mirrors the one that already exists on the display side.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: One, and it is the reason for measuring first. I expected the tilde marker to be degrading citations broadly, so I compared the held rate for marked and unmarked rows before touching anything: 5 of 474 marked rows held (1.05%) against 18 of 1,790 unmarked (1.01%). The same rate - so the marker is NOT a systemic citation regression, and this fix is worth 5 rows, not hundreds. The honest number is the small one.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: One re.sub line in scripts/citation_proof.code_groups and one test appended to the existing tests/test_citation_proof.py. No new file, no new helper, no query, no schema touched. code_groups is pure: it takes a ref string and returns tuples.
pre_impl.external_source_error: No external source is called by any of the three changes - citation_proof.code_groups, page_coverage.skipped_pages and ai_extractor.drop_figure_narrations are pure functions over strings and lists. The external dependency sits one layer out, in the extraction run these changes exist to unblock, and it failed for real on 2026-10-02: the reader returned RateLimitError 429 insufficient_quota, "You have no credits remaining", and dcp_extract_changed stopped with that error before reaching the enqueue step. That is the right behaviour and was verified by it happening: the chapter's 580 pending queue rows were left exactly as they were, nothing was written, and no partial extraction reached review. A reader that cannot be called produces no provisions, which is distinguishable from a reader that returns none - the latter raises ChunkLoss.
pre_impl.frontend_type: No frontend type changes, and no frontend change at all. The one place the frontend already knows about any of this is lib/citation-display.ts, which strips the same /~\d+$/ marker before showing a label; this PR makes the Python side agree with it rather than altering it. ref_number was and remains a non-null text column and provision_text a text column; nothing changes shape. The visible difference is narrower than a type: citation_status can now reach 'proven' for a row whose clause number is marked, so the UI shows a clause number where it previously showed the page. Both renderings already exist and are already exercised, so no deploy and no migration is needed - the next read serves it.
pre_impl.user_failure_mode: Three distinct ones, and they fail in different directions. (1) The marker bug failed SAFELY: a planner saw the page where a clause number could have been shown, because citation_status withholds an unproven number. Nothing wrong was served; a convenience was withheld, which is why it survived #1197 unnoticed. (2) The figure narrations would have failed SILENTLY and are the serious one: a planner would have read "Technical details for the removable placard show a 360 mm wide by 500 mm high panel mounted on a post, with an overall indicated height of 1400 mm" as the council's own control, with measurements the reader took off a drawing, attributed to Sydney DCP 2012 Schedule 6. There is no way to tell from the page that the council did not write that sentence. (3) The coverage false refusal failed VISIBLY and conservatively: the chapter was refused, so a planner saw City of Sydney schedules as it was before 1 October - stale, but sourced, dated and traceable. Cost is a stale chapter, never wrong text. All three are now one of: fixed, dropped before it can be reviewed, or correctly scored.

functions.name: code_groups
functions.input: a ref_number such as Sydney_DCP_2012__section_3_general_provisions__3_15_5_2~2; only the tail after the last '__' is read
functions.output: ordered (letter_prefix, [numeric parts]) groups, which split_ref turns into the clause number the page is searched for. With the fix the marked ref yields ('', ['3','15','5','2']) instead of ('', ['3','15','5']).
functions.if_none: split_ref returns an unjudged_reason instead of sections, and the row is reported as unjudged rather than proven - which is what 3_15~6 was getting ('bare integer section, not discriminating'). It fails toward withholding a clause number, never toward showing an unproven one.

functions.name: split_ref
functions.input: the same ref_number; it consumes code_groups' output and peels the trailing item marker
functions.output: (sections, item, unjudged_reason). The fix changes only which clause number arrives here; split_ref itself is untouched.
functions.if_none: returns 'no clause number in the ref' and the citation is unjudged, so nothing is claimed about it.

functions.name: drop_figure_narrations
functions.input: the provision dicts the reader returned, after the page-coverage re-read has run
functions.output: (kept, dropped). Dropped are provisions whose body opens with a report of what a drawing shows; the count and their codes are printed, so the removal is never silent.
functions.if_none: returns (provs, []) and nothing changes, which is the common case since 0 of 24,692 served rows match. Called after the re-read deliberately: a page whose only output was a narration still counts as read, so the drop cannot make it look skipped and refuse the chapter for the opposite reason.

functions.name: rule_lines
functions.input: a page's sentence lines, each already tokenised into words
functions.output: the lines carrying a rule word, or ALL of them when none does, so a page of pure narrative keeps the old scoring and the re-read trigger is no less sensitive there
functions.if_none: the fallback returns every line, which is the pre-change behaviour; it cannot return an empty list, so skipped_pages never divides by zero.

functions.name: skipped_pages
functions.input: page number -> that page's text lines, plus every text the reader returned
functions.output: the page numbers whose rule-bearing sentences are mostly absent. Page 65 goes from refused (14 of 47) to read (7 of 7 obligation lines, 7 of 13 rule-word lines).
functions.if_none: returns [] and no page is re-read or refused. A page under MIN_LINES is left out of judgement entirely, unchanged.

queries: N/A - code_groups and split_ref are pure string functions and this change adds no query. The measurements above read dcp_review_queue through the existing read-only scripts (dq_db.connect sets readonly).

break_it.scenario: A real clause number is mistaken for the marker and silently truncated - the exact trap #1197 names, since section 3.16 is stored as 3_16 and an underscore marker could not have been told apart from it.
break_it.what_happens: The clause number shown would be the parent instead of the clause, which is the DQ-111 class in reverse: a number that is wrong rather than withheld. That is worse than the bug being fixed, because an unproven number is hidden while a wrong one is shown.
break_it.how: The strip is anchored to a literal tilde followed by at least one digit and a word boundary, and a tilde cannot appear in a clause number - dcp_extract_changed is the only writer and it writes ~ only as the collision marker. The test pins x__3_16 explicitly: it still reads ['3.16'].

break_it.scenario: The marker shape changes - someone switches the suffix to ~a/~b, or to a bare ~ with no digit, or moves it to the front of the ref.
break_it.what_happens: The strip stops matching, the last clause component is eaten again, and marked rows quietly go back to never proving. Nothing fails loudly; the only symptom is held rows, which is how this bug survived #1197 in the first place.
break_it.how: Not mitigated, and deliberately not. Guarding against a marker shape the producer cannot emit would mean asserting on an input the system does not create. The pairing in the test is the real protection: every case asserts a marked ref against its unmarked twin, so whoever changes the marker only has to add their new shape to that list to find out.
break_it.repro: change the suffix in dcp_extract_changed.py:4032 and re-run the test

break_it.scenario: The fix makes previously-held rows prove with the WRONG clause number, i.e. it loosens the gate instead of correcting it.
break_it.what_happens: Rows would be approved carrying a clause number the council never printed, which is the DQ-111 fabricated-clause class reaching a reader.
break_it.how: Checked against the source rather than against our own output: the one clause number traced to the PDF, 3.15.5.2, is printed on the page the row cites. And the count discriminates - the re-grade moved exactly the 5 rows whose refs carry the marker, by name, and left all 18 unmarked held rows held. A loosened gate would have cleared some of those 18.
break_it.repro: python scripts/dcp_approve_graded.py --council city_of_sydney (dry run) - 18 held, 0 of them marked

break_it.scenario: A `~<digits>` sequence that is NOT the producer's trailing marker - `3_15~2.4` - is stripped anyway, and the remains parse as a clause number.
break_it.what_happens: `3_15~2.4` reads as `3.15.4`: a clause number that looks entirely plausible, invented out of a ref shape that should have stayed unjudged. DQ-111, from the fix meant to prevent it.
break_it.how: Raised by the Sol cross-review of the first version at confidence 0.96, and real: the unanchored strip did produce ['3.15.4']. Anchored to the end of the tail. Sol's own suggested fix, a single `~\d+$`, was not enough - dcp_extract_changed's `while f'{ref}~{suffix}' in new_provisions` can mark a ref that already carries a marker, and a single anchor leaves `X_5~2` out of `X_5~2~3`, bringing the eaten component straight back. Shipped `(?:~\d+)+$`, which is the only one of the three correct on both.

break_it.scenario: Narrowing the coverage denominator lets through the loss the guard was built for: a page of controls passes because its commentary came back while the controls did not.
break_it.what_happens: Printed rules are silently deleted from a chapter on approval. That is the Warringah case, 21 of 226 pages and 172 live rules whose words ARE printed, and Canterbury-Bankstown 6-2's 33 pages of objectives.
break_it.how: Run on the REAL page in all three directions rather than reasoned about: controls returned gives read; nothing returned is caught; only the commentary returned with the controls dropped is caught. A page whose rule lines are all absent still scores 0. And the refusal in _reread_skipped_pages is already gated on holds_rules (two or more obligation words), so a page with no rule words could never refuse a chapter today: narrowing the score changes the number on pages that already qualify, not which pages qualify.

break_it.scenario: The figure-narration rule deletes a genuine control because the council's own sentence mentions a drawing.
break_it.what_happens: A printed rule disappears from the chapter with no row for anybody to review, which is worse than a bad row because a bad row is visible.
break_it.how: Anchored to the body's opening rather than searching it, and that was decided BY the measurement: unanchored matched 9 live served rows and all 9 were genuine. The test pins the four confusable shapes as keepers - a mid-provision note about the council's own diagrams, "The diagram is to indicate ..." (a requirement on a submitted drawing), "Figure 12.1.2 shows ..." (how a council cites its own figure), and a control that merely ends "... as the drawing shows".

mutation_analysis: Two mutations, both run rather than described. (1) Delete the strip by restoring code_groups to its pre-fix body: 3 of the test's 4 marked/unmarked pairs fail, with the measured outputs ['3.15.5'] vs ['3.15.5.2'], ['3.1'] vs ['3.1.1'], and [] vs ['3.15']. The 4th pair, 7_4 (a)~2, passes either way - the test is not vacuous, and that one surviving pair is itself the finding, because it is the shape #1197 reasoned from. (2) Make the strip greedy, ~\d* or a bare ~.*: x__3_16 and the 7_4 (a)~2 pair still pass, so this test does NOT catch greediness. Accepted, because the marker's only writer always emits ~ plus an integer (dcp_extract_changed.py:4032), so no ~-without-digits ref exists to protect against and a test for one would assert on an impossible input. Two more after the Sol cross-review, both run on the three candidate patterns side by side: unanchored `~\d+ ` gives 3_15~2.4 -> ['3.15.4'] (invents a clause) while X_5~2~3 is correct; single-anchored `~\d+$` gives 3_15~2.4 -> ['3','4'] (correct, unjudged) but X_5~2~3 -> [] against X_5 -> ['5'] (wrong); shipped `(?:~\d+)+$` is the only one correct on both. Each failure is caught by a named assertion in test_the_marker_strip_is_anchored_and_repeatable, so neither half is vacuous. For the coverage change the mutation is the fixture itself, and it was involuntary: the first version of test_commentary_the_reader_rightly_skipped used 4 controls and 8 commentary lines, which is 4/12 = 0.333 all-lines - ABOVE PAGE_HIT, so the old scoring would not have refused it and the test asserted something untrue. It failed on the assertion that the old denominator refuses the page, and the fixture was rebuilt to the real page's shape (4 of 17 = 0.2353 all-lines, 4 of 5 rule-bearing). One commentary line in it carries a rule word on purpose; a fixture where none did would make the narrowing look cleaner than it is. For drop_figure_narrations the mutation is the anchor: remove it and the keeper test's four shapes are dropped instead of kept, which is the 9 live rows measured.
residual_risk: Rows graded before this fix keep their stale 'not proven' verdict until dcp_fidelity_gate.py is re-run for their chapter, and the gate only re-grades PENDING rows - so a marked row already approved or rejected keeps the old verdict and its clause number stays withheld rather than wrongly shown. That is the safe direction, but it means the benefit is not retroactive across the whole queue. This change does not touch the 18 City of Sydney rows that are genuinely unproven, and it does not change what citation_status displays - only which clause number gets checked. The two shapes the anchoring protects against do not exist in the queue today, checked rather than assumed: ref_number ~ '~[0-9]+.*~[0-9]+' returns 0 doubly-marked rows, and the 16 rows an earlier query flagged as 'text after the marker' turned out to be two-digit markers (~10 .. ~22), not trailing text - that first query was wrong and is recorded here because it nearly became a claim. So the tests pin the behaviour before such a ref appears, not after. The coverage change is the one with real residual risk, and it is this: a page whose controls are written without any of RULE_WORDS and without an item label is now scored against the fallback (every line), which is the old behaviour, so nothing is lost there - but a page MIXING such controls with rule-worded ones has them outside the denominator. No instance was found; the measurement that would settle it is a chapter where a known loss is confined to unworded controls, and none is to hand. The figure-narration rule's residual risk is narrower: it only ever drops, never rewrites, and the drop is printed with the codes, so a wrong drop shows up as a missing section in the review file rather than as wrong text served.

post_merge.db_reset: No. No schema or data change. The only database effect is indirect: re-running dcp_fidelity_gate.py rewrites fidelity_status/fidelity_detail on pending queue rows, which that script already does by design and which is re-runnable.
post_merge.secrets: None written or staged. A copy of the main checkout's .env was placed in the worktree so the extraction and the gate could reach R2 and the database; it is covered by .gitignore line 46 and git status never listed it.
post_merge.manual_verify: Yes, one thing, and it is specific: for any chapter whose queue holds ~-marked refs, run dcp_fidelity_gate.py then dcp_approve_graded.py and confirm the held count falls by the number of marked rows in the held set and by no more. A held count that falls further means the gate was loosened, which is the failure this change has to not be. Second thing, for the coverage change: the next chapter that refuses on PageLoss should be checked the way page 65 was - does a correct extraction of its rule-bearing lines score above PAGE_HIT? If a real loss ever stops being refused, this is the change that did it.
